newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Urban poverty seen cause of Indonesia violence.
newsitem.headline: Urban poverty seen cause of Indonesia violence.

text.p: Indonesia's election campaign has been hit by widespread violence because urban poor are using the opportunity to give vent to frustration with the country's economic and political system, analysts and diplomats said.

They said the scale of the violence in the campaign for the May 29 general elections was unprecedented in Indonesia's recent history, and blamed increasing disparities between the rich and the poor and the lack of escape valves to ease the frustration.

But the violence has been confined almost exclusively to Java, the most populous island in the sprawling 5,000 km (3,000 mile) archipelago and home to some 60 percent of the nation's 200 million people.
"Despite what the World Bank says about Indonesia's development, there is a considerable gap in income levels," said one diplomat on Wednesday.
"This had led to a lot of tension."

Indonesia's rigid political system under the sometimes ruthless rule of President Suharto does not allow for displays of dissent and the pressure-cooker atmosphere has become supercharged in the once-in-five years opportunity afforded by the election campaign, they said.

The government permits only three political parties -- the ruling Golkar, the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- to contest elections.
All of them are required to swear to abide by state ideology and refrain from open criticism of the government and the political system.

Campaigning is barred except during the allotted four-week period before general elections. Leaders of the two minority parties stress that they are not members of the opposition but appear unclear about their precise political status.

Most of the urban poor have flocked to PPP ranks, as have supporters of Megawati Sukarnoputri, the daughter of late founding president Sukarno, who was ousted from the PDI leadership last year by a government-backed faction and is barred from contesting the poll.
Although PPP leaders have close links with the ruling apparatus, the party is seen as the best of the three options by anti-government partisans, analysts said.

Easily angered by any perceived heavy-handedness by security forces or favouritism shown to Golkar, these groups have clashed with police and loyalists of the ruling party in Jakarta and other towns on Java since the start of the campaign.

The violence has intensified over the past four days as the campaign heads for its close on Friday. Police have fired tear gas and rubber bullets and used warning shots to disperse stone-throwing mobs in more than a dozen places.
Any symbol of authority is in danger of being targeted by the mobs, said independent analyst Arief Budiman.
"I hear that in Central Java, owners of government vehicles have replaced their official red licence plates with black ones so they cannot be identified," he said.

Political scientist Juwono Sudarsono, deputy governor of the government's National Resilience Institute, said much of the dissent sprang from perceptions that economic development during Suharto's three decades in power has been skewed.
"Golkar...is strongly identified with government policy, which is perceived to only benefit those who are well-connected and rich," he told Reuters recently.
"This is the only time in their life that they (protesters) can exercise some degree of defiance against authority, against the rich, against the middle class."
The analysts said Golkar was likely to win the election easily despite the violence but one diplomat warned that any suspicion of vote fraud could lead to more unrest.
According to government figures 14 percent of the population is now below the poverty line as opposed to 60 percent when Suharto took power in the mid-1960s.
The government has also said per capital income has risen 14-fold in the past three decades but many analysts say only a tiny fraction of the population have reaped the full benefits.
